#6242. The Right Tote Bag Is the Ultimate Travel Companion—These Are Our Editors’ Favorites

If you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option. From early morning flights to daily office commutes, or even a packed Saturday afternoon at the farmers market, our editors are always relying on their favorite tote. The best tote bags hold everything from our laptops, headphones, and water bottles to sleep masks and our most-used beauty products. Whether you reach for a structured leather version to pack your essential items in or an oversized, canvas carryall for a day at the park, the functions of the right tote are infinite.

Though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler. My favorite tote has been my everyday work bag for years, but it has also accompanied me on countless flights, weekend getaways, and last-minute happy hours. A reliable tote bag really can do it all. Keep reading to discover 15 of our editors' favorite tote bags and why we can’t live without them.

Coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager. Though I still cherish that tiny bag, my most used Coach item is my leather tote. For years, the Nina Tote bag has been my reliable sidekick. I’ve had it for so long that Coach no longer produces it. On the bright side, the Maggie Tote bag is almost identical to mine and is just as practical. I have put my bag through anything and everything over the years, and there is very little wear and tear. The leather is structured and durable, yet flexible enough to fit everything I need without toppling over. With plenty of interior pockets, my necessities all have a place, so I never have to go digging through the bottom of my bag to find the right lip gloss. Not only do I love traveling with this tote, but it’s also my everyday work bag and my go-to for almost every kind of activity.

I've never really had a work bag that I truly loved until I tried this one from Cuyana. What I appreciate about the System Tote are the additional organizational accessories that you can purchase to add a bit more structure to the interior. Aside from lugging it to and from the office each day, I use this tote as a personal item on the plane and brought it with me on a road trip to Acadia National Park, and have found it to be the ultimate travel companion. The built-in interior pocket is perfect for storing essentials you need to reach easily, like your passport, earbuds, or some petty cash, and since the bag can be snapped closed, you don't have to worry about anything flying out. —Jamie Spain, travel bookings editor

This bag is all about the pockets. No tote has ever kept me quite as organized as this one from MZ Wallace, a brand known for its signature quilted bags. It offers six interior pockets, five exterior pockets, and a detachable pouch, offering me a dedicated space for all of my essentials plus a whole lot more. I’m always impressed at how much this thing fits; an umbrella, my 13-inch laptop, a full change of clothes, and my lunch. The Medium Metro tote features ultra-soft shoulder straps, making it a go-to for commutes to the office. My favorite thing about this bag is how lightweight it feels even when full—it never digs into my shoulders or hurts my arms. More features that make this roomy tote a smart choice for travelers: a luggage sleeve, protective feet, and a detachable and adjustable crossbody strap. —Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

Monos’s Metro Tote has been with me longer than most New Yorkers are in relationships. I've received so many compliments on this gorgeous structured bag from Cuyana—it's been a great work bag, with plenty of space for my laptop, planner, Kindle, chargers, and other day-to-day essentials. I wasn't sure how well it would function as a personal item as there's not a zipper to fully close the bag, but on a flight to Aruba, I made use of the leather ties to keep items contained, and found it well-sized to slip under the seat in front of me, even with my toiletry bag and a sweatshirt stuffed inside. The bag is perfect in the way a red apple sitting on a teacher’s desk is perfect. It’s classic, without ornament, the kind of thing that expresses its utility in its design. It’s both ubiquitous and aspirational, stirring up images of a dreamy East Coast: a white-sand, Nantucket beach; a shabby, wood-planked boathouse on the coast of Maine; a Gothic-inspired Ivy League campus. I've used it as a carry-on item, a beach tote, and as a weekender. Baggu’s Nylon shoulder bag is more durable than its canvas tote bags but equally as stylish. It’s slightly slouchy, slightly structured, and comes in the signature Baggu colors and patterns. The adjustable quilted shoulder strap allows for a crossbody fit, a must-have for me when I’m commuting into the office or walking longer distances (nobody needs their laptop sliding off their shoulder onto the sidewalk). I find myself continuously reaching for this multipurpose tote on my way to the gym, office, farmers market, and airport. —Hannah Towey, associate editor

Just when I think I’ve run out of room, I haven’t. The expandable bottom of this Calpak laptop tote adds an extra four inches, allowing me to add last-minute essentials or souvenirs mid-trip. Like all products in the brand’s Luka collection, it’s made of a lightweight, ultra-soft, puffy exterior that makes carrying its handle easy. The material is also easy to clean—simply wipe away dirt or spills without a worry. Inside, there’s a padded 15" laptop sleeve, multiple side pockets, and a zippered section to keep smaller items organized. As a shopping writer who is constantly running between the office, press previews, catch ups with friends and, of course, the airport, I need a bag with space for all the day’s exploits and then some. July’s Juliette Soft Work Tote is my perfect do-it-all companion. Brushed gold hardware and a buttery-soft faux leather exterior mean it looks effortlessly chic at after-work drinks, and when I'm off to the airport, the removable trolley sleeve slides over my suitcase handle so I can breeze through the terminal. It is my favorite desk-to-departure tote bag. —Charley Ward, commerce writer, Condé Nast Traveller UK

My Strathberry Kite is my most-used travel accessory. Not only do I use it for day-to-day tasks, it comes with me on almost every trip (the exception being adventure travel), and most recently carried me through trips to Lisbon and Istanbul, where I spent weekends catching up with friends and sightseeing. It's an ideal size for a laptop, should you wish to take it, but fits in plenty of other necessary items, too (like flip-flops or ballet flats after hours of strolling through cobbled streets). I love the walnut color and the soft, supple leather. I'm sure this will be a favorite of mine for years to come. —Abigail Malbon, global audience development manager

When I first saw Parker Thatch offers its Jack Tote bag in this unique zebra and burgundy color combo, I knew it had to be mine. I found it online about a year ago, and it sold like hot cakes—and has been (devastatingly) sold out since. I received it as a sweet gift from my partner a few months ago, who had pre-ordered it to arrive right when it was back in stock. I've been using it as my go-to work bag ever since. It has an incredible amount of space and strength to carry all of my everyday essentials and then some—from my laptop and a book to makeup and toiletries. Because of its exterior fabric as hair-on cowhide, she just needs to be shielded from the rain a bit more than your average bag. If the design is calling your name on this bad boy, it’s well worth the splurge. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

I love anything Longchamp, and this gorgeous beach tote from the brand is my cherry on top of any vacation outfit. It’s large enough to hold a full day’s worth of goodies (sunscreen! sweatshirt! beach read!), but fits on the shoulder with ease. Plus, the toggle on the front keeps things contained in the most Longchamp-esque way. —H.C.

After passing the gauntlet of a last-minute trip to the British Virgin Islands, I always keep the Foldie Travel Bag on me, whether it’s riding in my backpack during my daily commute or stuffed into my suitcase on longer hauls. The front pocket easily held my thick reading list and two Moleskine classic notebooks; the full 40 liters of space in the main compartment (with the expansion unzipped) fit a week’s worth of clothes, chargers for four different devices, and another bag filled with toiletry bottles, plus room to spare for souvenirs. Another perk: the two inner pockets and wet pocket proved useful in sorting out the bag’s increasingly chaotic contents. The luggage sleeve was a relieving bonus that allowed me to transfer the hefty weight of my zealous packing to my suitcase. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations

I absolutely love this tote. Whether I’m wearing it to the office or while traveling, it fits everything I need. Plus, it comes with a separate removable pouch that I use even when I’m not wearing the bag. This slouchy bag is super durable and matches any outfit. —Pooja Nayyar, associate social media manager

Sentimentality may cloud my vision, for the tote in my possession belongs to my late grandmother. And when I tell you I was complimented frequently for it while in Italy, I mean I felt I needed to use the bag to beat back admirers waxing: “Wow, is Vera Bradley back?”; “Is it reversible?!”; “The textiles are so beautiful.” I often caught myself fantasizing about dumping it upside down to perform a “What’s in my bag” for nobody in particular—so capacious is the tote that I was needlessly carrying multiple novels within and rarely remembered to leave my toiletry kit on the hotel bathroom counter where it belonged. Handy pockets ringing the interior are just icing, and would have kept my passport safely inside had I ever been moved to act on the aforementioned dumping. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

#6241. Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

#6240. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6239. Why Virgin Atlantic Is Targeting The 40 RAF Pilots Keeping Britain's F-35 Fleet Flyable

jremes84 & Ian Cramman | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The United Kingdom only has around four dozen trained F-35B fighter jet pilots and around 150 Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet pilots. Losing even a handful of these hard-to-replace pilots to commercial airlines is painful. They are targeted by British airlines, with Virgin Atlantic directly targeting them in its recruitment ads in 2024.

As the Royal Air Force is so much smaller than the United States Air Force (and Marines/Navy), it lacks depth in pilots. Training an F-35 fighter jet pilot can cost around $10 million, and new pilots graduating annually in the UK are often measured in the single digits.

With that being said, airlines will typically focus more on military transport pilots, such as those flying A330 MRTTs and A400Ms. Let's examine how Virgin Atlantic seeks to attract ex-RAF pilots and why this is a major problem for the Royal Air Force (and Royal Navy).

In 2024, the publication London Loves Business wrote that "RAF pilots who have operated on F-35 B Lightning II and Typhoon FGR4 are being offered double their annual salary to join Virgin." It adds that those pilots would be given routes to Barbados and New York to quit the RAF and fly with Virgin Atlantic.

The report stated that the pilots were being offered around double the money that they would typically earn flying for the Royal Air Force. At the time, the Virgin Atlantic advert was reported to read as follows:

"In order to be suitable, you must be operating, or have operated in the last three years on one of the following RAF Aircraft: F-35 B Lightning II, Typhoon FGR4. As a member of our Flight Crew, you will be joining the UK’s only exclusively long-haul airline. Flying out of London Heathrow to exciting destinations such as New York, San Francisco, Las Vegas, Delhi, Barbados, Antigua, and many more."

The advert went on to say that Virgin Atlantic operates the "youngest, cleanest, and most technologically sophisticated" widebody aircraft. Virgin is unusual in exclusively operating a fleet of widebody aircraft. Airlines poaching trained fighter jet pilots is common in many countries, including the United States. For air forces, this can be devastating as it costs around ten million dollars to train a frontline fighter jet pilot and takes years to replace them.

In a typical Western air force, there should be around 1.3 to 1.5 trained pilots for every fast jet. That said, Britain (and other air forces) have struggled to maintain this figure. While the US military has around 37,000 military pilots, including in the USAF, Army (helicopters), Marines, Navy, and Coast Guard, the British military likely has around 2,500.

Of these, around 1,500 are in the RAF and 500 are each in the Royal Navy and British Army. In 2014, the British Government revealed that there were 1,760 trained regular pilots in the RAF (excluding reserves and other aircrew), although that number has likely declined somewhat over the last decade. However, fighter jet pilots are a small subset of the overall group of pilots.

In late 2022, former Defense Secretary Ben Wallace revealed there were only 30 qualified British F-35 pilots, plus three exchange pilots. By 2023, that number had risen to 34, with seven more soon to graduate. By mid-2026, the RAF had received all of its initially ordered 48 F-38Bs, minus one that fell off an aircraft carrier.

Ideally, the RAF should have around 60–70 or so trained F-35B pilots, but it is unclear how many there are. There have been reports that the ratio may be closer to one pilot per jet, suggesting the RAF may now have somewhere around 45 to 50 trained F-35B pilots. Headlines will often talk about the fighter jets, how many there are, and how ready they are, but pilot availability is often a more pressing bottleneck.

The RAF procured a total of 137 Eurofighter Typhoons. Of these, 26 of the Tranche 1 fighter jets have now been retired, leaving a fleet of four remaining. These are stationed at RAF Mount Pleasant in the Falkland Islands as the UK's farthest air base with a permanent fighter jet presence. They are tasked with defending the islands from Argentina and are supported by A400Ms and A330 MRTTs.

The remaining Typhoons include 67 Tranche 2 and 40 Tranche 3 fighter jets. In January 2026, the British Government stated it would upgrade 40 of them with new radars and other systems. In July 2026, the budget was significantly increased, and it was reported that all would be upgraded. Britain had previously said the remaining four Tranche 1 fighter jets would retire in 2027, but now it is unclear.

Select aircraft of the Royal Air Force (per RAF)

There has not been an equivalent public disclosure for how many Typhoon fighter jet pilots are serving in the RAF. A reasonable range would be 140-160 trained Typhoon pilots. This would give the RAF a group of up to 200 fast jet pilots in total. Additionally, as of June 2026, the Royal Air Force had 119 trainee fast-jet pilots progressing through the training pipeline, from RAF Cranwell to the point of starting an Operational Conversion Unit.

Beginning around 2015 and then accelerating after COVID-19, the US airline industry has faced an unprecedented pilot shortage. This has affected regional airlines in particular and is made worse by retiring baby boomers. In response, the industry moved to attract former US military helicopter pilots; previously, the focus had been on fixed-wing pilots.

One of the most famous examples was that of Frontier Airlines, which launched its Rotor Transition Program to help military helicopter pilots transition and receive their fixed-wing qualifications. The program ended up being so successful that, Frontier's website said:

"Due to the overwhelmingly positive response and large number of applications we received for our Rotor Transition Program, we have temporarily closed the application window. Keep an eye out for more information regarding the application window opening and future recruitment events."

Meanwhile, there has not been the same recruitment drive in the UK, as the UK airline industry is much smaller, the military is much smaller (only a few hundred helicopter pilots), and converting is less straightforward. Instead, British industry focuses on recruiting former RAF transport pilots, fast jet pilots, airline cadets, and airline pilots from other airlines.

Why do airlines pay A350 and Boeing 777 Captains the same, even though no US carrier operates both of the aircraft types?

In both the United States and the United Kingdom, it is relatively straightforward for fighter jet pilots to transition from flying fixed-wing military aircraft to flying commercial passenger jets. With that being said, the United States has built a considerably more mature and streamlined process.

For ex-British fast-jet pilots, the primary challenge is obtaining the civilian licenses, certifications, and experience required by the UK Civil Aviation Authority. The CAA does recognize military flying experience through its Military Aircrew Accreditation Scheme, meaning that transitioning pilots do not need to start from scratch.

They can get credits toward their Commercial Pilot License, but still generally need to complete their ATPL theoretical knowledge tests, civilian flight tests, and so on. The entire process of converting from military to commercial jets often takes six to twelve months, depending on how much training credit is granted and the airline course start date.

In the US, the process typically takes around three to nine months. For comparison, for those starting from scratch in the UK, it typically takes three to over eight years for a pilot to fly with a major airline. It's between two and over six years in the United States, depending on various factors.

According to Planespotters.net, Virgin Atlantic currently operates an all-widebody fleet of 44 aircraft with an average age of 8.4 years. These include 14 Airbus A330s (six A330-300s and nine A330neos), 12 Airbus A350-1000s, and 17 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. This makes it one of the largest all-widebody fleets in the world, although, for comparison, this total would only represent around 15% of Emirates' giant all-widebody fleet.

Virgin Atlantic's outstanding A330-900 orders will replace its remaining fleet of legacy A330-300s by 2027 while growing the overall fleet. The airline was established in 1984 and serves around 29 destinations, mostly from its hubs at London Heathrow and Manchester. The airline is also a member of SkyTeam and is 49% owned by Delta Air Lines. Virgin Atlantic has evolved into a mixed network carrier that serves both leisure-heavy destinations and business-heavy routes.

It offers flights to Caribbean destinations like Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Grenada, Jamaica (Montego Bay), Mexico's Cancun, St. Lucia, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines. Its US destinations include Las Vegas, Orlando, Miami, Tampa, as well as some other less leisure-heavy destinations, such as Boston. Virgin has flights on some other non-leisure routes, including to India and Nigeria.

#6238. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

#6235. The Manufacturing Decision Boeing Was Forced To Make When It Developed The 737 MAX

In August 2011, Boeing officially launched its 737 MAX program after American Airlines made the historic decision to split its once all-Boeing fleet and buy 50% of its next-generation narrowbodies from Airbus. AA was facing rising fuel expenses and operating an aging fleet of roughly 300 McDonnell Douglas MD-80 jets. Thus, in July of that same year, AA revealed that of the 460 jets it planned to procure to modernize its fleet, 260 would be from the A320 family.

By mid-2011, Airbus had accumulated more than 1,000 orders for its re-engined A320neo. The airline chose to award more than half of its future fleet slots to Airbus because it already had a production-ready jet. In the aftermath, Boeing leadership abandoned plans for an all-new composite narrowbody within hours. Developing a new mainline jet would have required an estimated $10 billion to $12 billion and up to a decade of research. Instead, it committed to developing a re-engined 737 to retain its portion of the order.

Modifying the legacy 737 airframe was estimated to cost a third as much, with initial deliveries expected in 2017. Boeing also pursued certification as a derivative of the original 1967 type to entice operators with a cheap transition, even earning a $1 million per-aircraft rebate from launch customer Southwest Airlines. However, preserving grandfathered handling characteristics while integrating larger, higher-bypass turbofans onto the low-slung 1960s airframe imposed engineering constraints that forced Boeing to make a fateful compromise: the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System.

At first, Boeing executives James Albaugh and Jim McNerney placed a wager on the Yellowstone Project, believing that airlines would wait for a 2020 clean-sheet composite plane instead of using the Airbus A320neo. Instead, to immediately save 15% on fuel consumption, operators quickly acquired more than 1,000 European narrowbodies. McNerney was then forced to abandon the Yellowstone study over the course of one weekend after American Airlines CEO Gerard Arpey threatened to terminate the airline's exclusive purchase agreement unless Boeing promptly supplied a re-engined 737.

Following the 737 MAX's formal debut on August 30, 2011, commercial contracts obliged Boeing to follow an accelerated derivative timetable. Southwest Airlines, the first client, ordered 150 aircraft in December 2011 under an arrangement that called for a $1 million rebate per plane if regulators imposed pilot simulator training. With Southwest eventually buying over 240 airframes, avoiding hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties necessitated certifying the 737 MAX using its original 1967 type certificate on a tight timetable.

Aerodynamic concessions were necessary to meet that deadline while mounting larger CFM International LEAP-1B engines onto the low-slung 1960s airframe. At high angles of attack, an uncontrollable nose-up pitching tendency was produced by cantilevering the nacelles forward and upward. Engineers used the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System software to digitally mask the pitch anomaly, accelerating delivery while introducing a single-sensor flight control vulnerability, instead of implementing structural wing modifications that would cause certification delays and simulator training.

Boeing engineers had to extend the nose landing gear on the 737 MAX by 8 inches (20 cm) more than the Next Generation series, as well as cantilever the nacelles forward and upward using structural titanium pylons in order to fit 69-inch (175 cm) CFM International LEAP-1B engines onto the low-slung 1967 737 airframe. These larger engine cowls, which were positioned above the wing chord, produced excess aerodynamic lift ahead of the center of gravity at high angles of attack, creating an uncontrollable nose-up pitching tendency that went against federal regulations for linear control column force progression toward an aerodynamic stall.

Rather than executing costly structural wing redesigns or installing mechanical counterweights, Boeing relied on the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System software to automatically command nose-down horizontal stabilizer trim without pilot input. To preserve grandfathered type-certificate commonality and avoid simulator training penalties, program officials positioned the software as a minor modification to the existing speed trim system and obtained Federal Aviation Administration approval to strip all references to the system from flight crew manuals, leaving operators and pilots unaware of its existence.

During certification flight testing, Boeing engineers increased the software's ability at lower airspeeds to push the horizontal stabilizer by 2.5 degrees based on input from a single angle-of-attack sensor, without reassessing single-point failure dangers. Boeing withheld internal simulator data from the Federal Aviation Administration, demonstrating that a company test pilot took more than 10 seconds to diagnose and counter an uncommanded activation, a delay classified as catastrophic internally when compared to the four-second federal response standard.

How the 767 is bridging the gap to a new generation of widebody twinjets in its twilight.

Boeing's Yellowstone Project originally divided commercial fleet renewal into three clean-sheet phases: Y1 for narrowbodies, Y2 for mid-sized jets, and Y3 for widebodies. While Y2 materialized as the composite 787 Dreamliner, severe delays and cost overruns on that program exhausted Boeing's engineering capacity and capital for Y1 and Y3. Simultaneously, Y1 studies stalled when engine manufacturers elected to frame their next-generation turbofans around the A320neo and air carriers ran out of patience, turning to the European planemaker.

Abandoning Y1 for a modified 737 forced engineers to integrate modern high-bypass engines on a fuselage created for 1960s crashworthiness and operating regulations. Grandfathering the type certificate allowed the 737 MAX to use older mechanical flight controls rather than adopt modern fly-by-wire. Thus, engineers could only use software-driven flight controls to a limited extent in compensating for the aircraft's size and weight. Instead, they modified the existing mechanical Speed Trim System with MCAS, using its jackscrew to move the horizontal stabilizer.

This reliance on grandfathered systems created direct performance gaps that a clean-sheet Y1 design would have eliminated through new systems and certification criteria. Unlike the 787, which features a digital alert system, the 737 MAX retained legacy warning lights and its AOA disagree alert. Disastrously, Boeing engineers discovered in August 2017 that the AOA alert was inoperable on more than 80% of delivered aircraft. Management deferred an MCAS software patch until 2020 and withheld the defect from operators and regulators until after the fatal crash in October 2018 of Lion Air Flight 610.

Shareholders have some serious questions for the manufacturer.

To reclaim narrowbody market share lost to the Airbus A320neo, Boeing structured the 737 MAX around minimizing airline transition costs and preserving existing fleet infrastructure. The high-bypass turbofans of the A320neo achieved 15% better fuel efficiency than the 737 NG thanks to large volumes of air around the engine core. Boeing required a very wide front fan diameter on its 737 MAX to match that, a design criterion that clashed with the 737's low ground clearance.

Boeing commercial leadership recognized that any derivative aircraft requiring full-flight simulator sessions would forfeit sales to legacy 737 operators. These commercial imperatives were codified directly into customer purchase agreements, most notably SWA's 240-strong order that included a $1 million rebate per delivered aircraft. Consequently, Boeing set minimal difference training as a core program objective. That meant pilot transition instruction from the 737 NG would be just a computer-based course, avoiding the expense of building and certifying new full-flight simulators before service entry.

Thus, to preserve the 1967 type certificate and avoid costly landing gear and wing-box redesigns, CFM International constrained the LEAP-1B to a 69-inch fan (175 cm) and a 9:1 bypass ratio, using 18 carbon-fiber composite blades to reduce rotational mass. Even with a flattened nacelle bottom, fitting the 6,129-pound (2,780 kg) engines required lengthening the nose gear by 8 inches (20 cm) and cantilevering the powerplants forward and upward on titanium pylons.

Positioned ahead of and above the wing chord, these enlarged cowls generated excess aerodynamic lift at high angles of attack, inducing an uncommanded nose-up pitching tendency that violated federal stall-recovery handling standards. Because extensive wing modifications would have invalidated the standing type certificate and triggered mandatory simulator retraining, Boeing engineers compensated digitally through MCAS to command 2.5 degrees of nose-down trim using data from a single external angle-of-attack vane.

The software enabled the airframe to meet certification handling rules on paper, but leadership went on to lobby the FAA to omit the software from flight crew manuals and differences tables, so Boeing could secure Level B training approval to win back airline orders. A conventional runaway stabilizer shows trim wheel rotation that pilots can recognize and disable. Meanwhile, MCAS was in discrete increments, and omitting the system deprived flight crews of the diagnostic knowledge to distinguish it as the source of a malfunction.

The families of those who perished continue to seek justice.

That software reliance was predetermined by 737 sales contracts negotiated years before the prototype flew. Southwest Airlines, the first customer, ordered 150 737 MAX aircraft in December 2011, with the agreement that Boeing would pay a $1 million rebate per jet if the Federal Aviation Administration permitted simple, simulator-based training for pilots migrating from the 737 NG to the MAX. With Southwest eventually buying over 240 airframes, avoiding hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties forced leadership to maintain common type ratings and remove system references from manuals.

During the initial 737 MAX 8 flight test campaign starting in January 2016, Boeing originally designed the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System to operate exclusively during high-speed, flaps-up wind-up turns. Lift generated by the forward-mounted CFM International LEAP-1B28 nacelles lightened control column forces as angle of attack increased, violating FAA stall characteristic parameters. Subsequently, software authority was extended to lower airspeeds by developers, allowing 2.5 degrees of nose-down horizontal stabilizer trim based on single-sensor AOA input.

In 2017, 737 Chief Technical Pilot Mark Forkner emailed the FAA Seattle Aircraft Evaluation Group requesting permission to remove references to the MCAS from the Flight Crew Operations Manual, unaware of the extended speed range of MCAS authority. In November 2016, Forkner discovered the system activating aggressively at lower airspeeds in simulator testing, claiming he had unknowingly misled regulators. Yet, Boeing officials never briefed the Seattle Aircraft Evaluation Group on the expanded low-speed authority or corrected their earlier operational representations.

#6234. American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami

A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

“Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”

American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card is a solid option for travelers who want to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

While it offers access to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners, its earning rate of 1.25 miles per dollar on most purchases and limited travel perks may leave some travelers wanting more.

Still, I think the VentureOne is worth considering if you're new to transferable rewards and aren't ready to commit to a more expensive travel card. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards is a no-annual-fee travel rewards card that earns Capital One miles.

The biggest draw here is the ability to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee. You can get more value from your rewards by transferring miles to airline and hotel partners, or redeem them at a fixed rate toward travel purchases if you'd rather keep things simple.

The card doesn't charge foreign transaction fees and comes with a few travel perks, including complimentary Hertz Gold+ Rewards Five Star status.*

That said, the VentureOne's everyday earning rate is on the lower side. I'd recommend it primarily to travelers who want access to Capital One's transfer partners without paying an annual fee, rather than those looking to earn the most rewards on everyday spending.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: The best Capital One credit cards to add to your wallet

Related: How to choose the best credit card for you

The VentureOne doesn't offer the extensive travel benefits of its higher-tier counterparts, but it still has a handful of perks worth knowing about.

One of the VentureOne's most useful benefits is that it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees.

Some credit cards charge around 3% on purchases made abroad, which can add up over the course of an international trip.

With the VentureOne, you can make international purchases without worrying about additional card fees.

Related: Best credit cards with no foreign transaction fees

VentureOne cardholders can enroll in complimentary Hertz Gold+ Rewards Five Star status.

Normally, earning this status requires completing three rentals or spending $1,000 on eligible rentals in a calendar year.

This status can provide benefits such as vehicle upgrades when available and additional rewards on eligible rentals.

While I wouldn't recommend choosing the VentureOne solely for this perk, it's a nice addition for travelers who occasionally rent cars.

The VentureOne also includes several protections that may come in handy when traveling or making purchases.

These include auto rental insurance, extended warranty protection and travel and emergency assistance.

For coverage details, including terms and exclusions, refer to your card's guide to benefits. These aren't necessarily benefits you'll use regularly, but they can provide some reassurance.

Related: The best credit cards for purchase protection

One of the VentureOne's biggest advantages is that it earns flexible Capital One miles rather than rewards tied to a single airline or hotel program.

That gives you several ways to use your rewards, depending on how much effort you want to put into maximizing them.

The VentureOne earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 1.25 miles per dollar spent on everyday purchases.

To put that into perspective, spending $1,000 on everyday purchases would earn you 1,250 miles. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuation of 1.85 cents per Capital One mile, those miles would be worth approximately $23 when maximized through transfer partners.

That's not a particularly strong return, especially when other no-annual-fee cards offer higher earning rates.

Still, the VentureOne keeps things simple. You don't have to keep track of rotating bonus categories, and you'll earn miles on every purchase.

If you're more concerned with earning transferable miles without paying an annual fee than maximizing every dollar you spend, that might be enough for you.

Related: How to earn, redeem and transfer Capital One miles

One of the easiest ways to use your Capital One miles is to use them to pay for eligible purchases as a statement credit.

You'll get a fixed value of 1 cent per mile, meaning 20,000 miles would cover a $200 travel purchase. This can be especially useful for expenses that aren't always easy to book with traditional airline or hotel points, such as Airbnb stays or Uber rides.

I like this option for beginners because there's no need to search for award availability or figure out how different loyalty programs work. You can just make an eligible travel purchase with your card and use your miles to cover it afterward.

You can also redeem your miles for Amazon purchases, Capital One entertainment purchases, cash back and gift cards. However, these options generally offer less value than travel redemptions, so I'd stick with using miles for travel whenever possible.

Related: How to get the maximum value when redeeming Capital One miles

If you're willing to put in a little more effort, transferring your Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners can be a great way to get more value from your rewards.

Capital One has more than 15 transfer partners, including programs like Avianca LifeMiles, British Airways Club and Choice Privileges. Most transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, although some partners have different ratios.

Personally, I love transferring Capital One miles to airline partners like Virgin Atlantic Flying Club and Air France-KLM Flying Blue.

For example, I recently transferred 6,400 Capital One miles to Flying Blue to book a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN) to Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS). I paid just $10.70 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost $163.95.

That worked out to about 2.39 cents per mile, well above TPG's valuation of Capital One miles. And while I booked through Flying Blue, I actually flew on Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) — a good example of how you can use one airline's miles to book flights on its partners.

Of course, not every transfer will give you that kind of value. I always recommend comparing the cash price of a flight to the number of miles you'd need to transfer.

I'd also avoid transferring miles before you have a specific redemption in mind, since transfers generally can't be reversed. Instead, find the flight you want, confirm award availability and then transfer your miles.

If you're new to points and miles, redeeming miles to cover travel purchases might be an easier place to start. But once you're comfortable with the basics, learning how to use transfer partners can really help you stretch your rewards further.

Related: How to transfer Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners

The VentureOne's biggest drawback is its relatively low everyday earning rate.

Earning 1.25 miles per dollar may be simple, but several competing cards offer higher returns without charging an annual fee — more on that below.

The VentureOne also lacks many of the travel benefits that make premium rewards cards appealing, including airport lounge access and annual travel credits.

If you travel frequently or put a significant amount of spending on your credit cards, you may find that paying an annual fee for a more rewarding card makes sense.

Related: How to decide if a credit card’s annual fee is worth paying

If you're considering the VentureOne, I'd also take a look at the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Both cards earn transferable Capital One miles, but the Venture Rewards earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, compared to the VentureOne's 1.25 miles per dollar spent. It also comes with a few additional travel perks, including up to a $120 statement credit every four years for the application fee for either Global Entry or TSA PreCheck

The trade-off is that the Venture Rewards has a $95 annual fee, while the VentureOne doesn't charge one.

Still, depending on how much you spend, that $95 could be worth paying. Based on TPG's valuation of 1.85 cents per Capital One mile, you'd need to spend about $6,850 a year on purchases earning the base rate for the extra miles to offset the Venture Rewards card's annual fee.

That's before factoring in welcome offers or other benefits. And if you typically redeem miles for travel statement credits at 1 cent apiece, you'd need to spend more to make up the difference.

Personally, I'd lean toward the Venture Rewards if you plan to use your card regularly and want to earn miles faster. But if avoiding an annual fee is your priority, the VentureOne still gives you access to the same transfer partners.

Related: Capital One Venture vs. VentureOne: Which card is right for you?

I think the VentureOne is worth considering if your priority is earning transferable travel rewards without paying an annual fee.

However, if you spend heavily on your card or travel frequently, the Venture Rewards or another higher-earning card could provide better long-term value.

There are currently two welcome offers available on the VentureOne, each with a different spending requirement:

Based on TPG's valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, these bonuses are worth $370 and $740, respectively.

The biggest difference between the two offers, aside from the bonus miles and spending requirements, is that the standard VentureOne offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74% (a balance transfer fee applies). The Miles Boost version doesn't offer this benefit.

Compared to the card's offer history, the standard 20,000-mile bonus has been available for most of the past few years, although Capital One briefly added a $100 travel credit to the offer in 2025.

The Miles Boost offer, on the other hand, matches the highest bonus we've seen on the VentureOne. So if you've been considering this card, now could be a particularly good time to apply for that version.

Personally, I'd lean toward the Miles Boost offer if you can comfortably meet the higher spending requirement and don't need the introductory APR benefit. You'll earn twice as many bonus miles for an additional $500 in spending.

Keep in mind that Capital One has a 48-month welcome bonus restriction across its Venture card family. If you've received a new cardmember bonus on the VentureOne, Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card within the past 48 months, you won't be eligible for another VentureOne bonus.

However, earning a VentureOne bonus doesn't, on its own, prevent you from qualifying for a future Venture Rewards or Venture X welcome bonus.

Related: Evaluating the current offer on the Capital One VentureOne

The VentureOne isn't the only option for travelers who want to earn rewards without paying a high annual fee. Depending on your spending habits and travel goals, one of these cards could be a better fit.

For additional options, check out our full list of the best no-annual-fee cards.

The Capital One VentureOne offers something you won't find on every no-annual-fee card: the ability to earn miles that transfer directly to airline and hotel partners.

That makes it a reasonable starting point for travelers who want to explore transferable rewards without committing to an annual fee.

However, its modest earning rate makes it harder to recommend to anyone looking to maximize rewards on everyday spending.

If you're comfortable paying a modest annual fee, I'd consider the Venture Rewards instead. But if avoiding an annual fee is your top priority and you want access to Capital One's transfer partners, the VentureOne is worth a look.

#6232. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6231. American Airlines Turns Back 10-Hour Flight To Buenos Aires After Lavatory Overflows

An American Airlines Boeing 777 flying from Dallas/Fort Worth to Buenos Aires returned to its departure airport on Friday night after a lavatory overflowed on board. Flight AA997 — operated by a 26-year-old 777-200ER — turned back over the Gulf of Mexico and landed at Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) just over two hours after taking off, with most of its scheduled 10-and-a-half-hour journey still ahead.

While airlines are allowed to operate aircraft with some lavatories out of service, these rules cover known faults before departure, and inoperative lavatories must be locked and marked as out of service. Problems that develop mid-flight are a different issue — for example, last month, another American 777-200ER was forced to divert after six of its eight lavatories stopped working.

Flight AA997 was scheduled to depart DFW at 7:30 PM local time on November 20 and arrive at Ezeiza International Airport (EZE) at 9:00 AM the following morning. Flight tracking data shows the aircraft departed 42 minutes late at 8:12 PM, before heading south over the Gulf of Mexico. However, it turned back toward Dallas around an hour into the flight, eventually landing back at DFW at 10:20 PM.

In a post on X, Flightradar24 reported that the aircraft returned to DFW because of a "lavatory overflow." The aircraft involved, registered N782AN, is a Boeing 777-200ER built in 2000. American has not disclosed how many passengers and crew were on board or what caused the overflow. Simple Flying has contacted the airline for comment and will update this story accordingly.

Returned to DFW after a lavatory overflow and landed safely

American operates a daily flight between Dallas/Fort Worth and Buenos Aires, scheduling the Boeing 777-200ER on the route this winter. DFW is one of three American gateways to Buenos Aires alongside New York JFK Airport (JFK), which has one daily Boeing 777-300ER service, and Miami International Airport (MIA), which has two daily flights.

Minimum equipment lists (MELs) allow some lavatories on board a commercial plane to be out of service. However, the plumbing must be isolated to prevent leaks, and the door must be locked and signed as out of service. An overflow incident represents a biohazard risk, possibly spreading wastewater outside the lavatory and onto the cabin floor.

There are also concerns that a leak could affect onboard electrical systems, potentially creating additional safety issues. American's 777-200ERs are equipped with 273 seats – 37 in business class, 24 in premium economy and 212 in economy – and typically have eight lavatories. On a full flight, that works out to around 34 passengers per lavatory.

Returning to Dallas brought the aircraft back to American's largest hub, where the airline has maintenance teams and spare widebodies to help get passengers moving again. With fuel on board for a flight lasting more than 10 hours, it remains unclear whether the crew dumped fuel before landing or carried out an overweight landing, which would require a maintenance inspection.

Airplanes keep lavatory ashtrays not for comfort but as a mandated, last-line safety tool—ensuring safe disposal of illicit lit cigarettes

Friday evening's return to DFW comes around six weeks after another American 777-200ER diverted because of lavatory problems. On October 6, flight AA37 from Madrid Airport (MAD) to Dallas diverted to New York JFK after all but two of its eight lavatories stopped working. The FAA reported at the time that the pilots cited "an inadequate number of operational lavatories" as the reason for the diversion. The aircraft had 287 people on board and spent almost three and a half hours on the ground at JFK before continuing to Dallas.

The turnback also comes just over a week after a lavatory problem forced a Frontier Airlines flight to declare an emergency. On November 11, flight F93566 from Denver to Detroit diverted to Chicago O’Hare after a leaking faucet in a forward lavatory flooded the cabin floor. In an air traffic control recording, the crew declared a Mayday, adding that they were "worried about electronics."

#6230. Lufthansa Ordered The Airbus A350-1000 In 2023 & Got It Before The Boeing 777-9 It Ordered In 2013

Lufthansa is set to be the launch customer for the upcoming Boeing 777-9. The problem, however, is that it was scheduled to enter service in 2020. The entry-into-service date for the 777-9 has been pushed back several times, and the aircraft has become one of the most delayed projects in commercial aviation history. What's more, the 777-9 is not a new aircraft; rather, it's an overhaul of an existing aircraft type (albeit an extremely thorough one). The 777-9's EIS is now set for 2027.

In 2023, Lufthansa ordered the Airbus A350-1000. While the A350-1000 competes with the 777-9, Lufthansa will operate both in complementary roles. Strikingly, Lufthansa has already received its first A350-1000, with the first example having been delivered in November 2026. The German flag carrier ordered the A350-1000 a full ten years after it first placed its orders for the 777-9, yet its first A350-1000 has arrived a few months before the first 777-9 is set to be delivered, and this assumes that the current 2027 timeline will stick.

Lufthansa first ordered the 777-9 in 2013, initially placing 34 orders for the aircraft. Interestingly, this was the first time the airline had ordered a passenger variant of the 777, and it will be the first to operate the type once it's ready. In 2019, Lufthansa converted 14 of its firm orders to options, leaving it with 20 firm orders and 24 options for the 777-9. In addition, Lufthansa Group also holds orders for seven 777-8Fs to be operated by Lufthansa Cargo, and it will be the first European operator of the aircraft.

The group ordered ten A350-1000s in 2023, as part of a larger order that included five A350-900s and seven Boeing 787s. The A350-1000 order was later increased to 15 units, and they will mainly operate out of Munich. Lufthansa took its first A350-1000 in November 2026, and including subsequent A350-900 orders, the airline group has ordered 75 A350s in total, split between 60 A350-900s and 15 A350-1000s.

While the A350-1000 will primarily be a Munich aircraft, the 777-9 is mainly intended to operate out of Frankfurt, and it will initially replace the airline's Boeing 747-400 fleet. While the configuration has not been officially revealed, the 747-400s that will be replaced by the 777-9s feature a relatively dense configuration with no first class cabin. As such, some of the airline's 777-9s may have only a three-class interior, while others may be delivered with a four-class layout and first class.

Despite being in development for nearly 14 years, the 777-9 is still not certified. The program has repeatedly encountered setbacks, and there have been multiple delays to the aircraft's certification. Boeing hoped to start delivering the 777-9 in 2020, but now anticipates that the aircraft will begin being delivered to customers in 2027. Lufthansa, meanwhile, has removed the 777-9 from internal planning for the 2027 summer schedule, meaning that it does not expect to have received a significant number of 777-9s, if any at all, before the season ends.

The aircraft's certification was heavily impacted by the two fatal Boeing 737 MAX 8 crashes in 2018 and 2019, which led to a 20-month grounding of the 737 MAX worldwide. Boeing faced increased scrutiny from the FAA following the tragic crashes, including closer oversight of the 777-9 certification program. COVID stretched out the timeline again, and multiple engineering and design challenges have further delayed the aircraft's certification.

The 777-9 features several new design elements that make it quite different from earlier 777 models. This includes a new carbon-composite wing, new engines, a fuselage stretch, a thoroughly updated cabin, and more. This means there are more variables with the 777-9 than with a project like the Airbus A320neo, where almost everything was identical to its predecessors apart from the engines.

Most recently, the FAA shifted resources towards certifying the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10, which are now ready to fly. With the two new 737 variants approved to enter service when ready, the FAA can allocate more resources to the 777-9 program. In addition, General Electric is awaiting FAA approval on a new mid-seal design for the GE9X, while certification flights are still ongoing.

Lufthansa has set Boeing an ultimatum ahead of its incoming widebody order.

Unlike most customers for the aircraft, Lufthansa doesn't plan to use the 777-9 as its flagship aircraft. Instead, the 747-8 will remain in this role, with Lufthansa operating 17 examples out of its Frankfurt hub, all of which will receive new interiors. The 20 777-9s will slot underneath the 747-8s. In Frankfurt, Lufthansa is also operating the 787-9, which will serve as its smallest widebody to operate thinner routes, along with some A350-900s. Meanwhile, the airline will operate most A350-900s out of Munich, alongside the A350-1000 and the Airbus A380.

The airline is currently flying just three Airbus A330-300s, which are set to be transferred to other airlines within Lufthansa Group by the end of the year. In addition, there are still six 747-400s flying and 11 A340-300s, which are meant to be fully retired by 2028 as the carrier takes more 777-9s and 787-9s. Furthermore, Lufthansa is operating eight A380s, which are receiving new business class seats that are different from the new Allegris interiors, and they should remain in service until the 2030s.

Lufthansa Current Widebody Fleet (Planespotters.net)

Looking ahead, Lufthansa's fleet will center on the A350-900 family and the 787-9, with the A350-900s mainly concentrated in Munich and the 787s based in Frankfurt. The 777-9s and 747-8s will remain Lufthansa's larger options for routes out of Frankfurt, while the equivalent for Munich will be the A350-1000 and A380-800. The A380s should be the next aircraft type to go in the 2030s, while the 747-8 is expected to remain in the fleet long-term.

While the seat count by cabin has yet to be revealed, the 777-9s will feature Lufthansa's Allegris interiors. The 777-9 was originally meant to launch the Allegris seats in 2020, but delays with the program led Lufthansa to introduce the seats on the A350-900 four years after their intended launch. For the most part, the Allegris cabins are the same for different aircraft from a customer experience standpoint (although different suppliers manufacture the seats for different aircraft).

The new first class cabins feature one row with three suites across, while the suites themselves offer near-ceiling-height partitions and sliding doors, along with modernized technology and in-suite climate controls. Uniquely, the center suite is sized to accommodate two passengers traveling together as a couple, with two seats side by side, a larger monitor, and double-bed capability. In a sense, it's one suite that can accommodate two passengers, which is a very unusual proposition.

There are a lot of moving parts at the German flag carrier.

The A350-1000 and 777-9 are competitors in the sense that they're the largest aircraft sold by Airbus and Boeing. But while airlines do compare them, they have significant differences, the most obvious being size. The 777-9 is much larger than the A350-1000 or the 777-300ER, and it can carry nearly as many passengers as the 747-400. The A350-1000 has lower trip costs and greater range, but the 777-9 has lower seat-mile costs and greater cargo volume.

Because these aircraft are quite compelling in different ways, several airlines have elected to buy both rather than choose. The A350-1000 can serve as a large ultra-long-range aircraft, while the 777-9 is typically bought for its floor space to serve as a flagship aircraft. Lufthansa has installed a first class cabin on its A350-1000s, but it's actually the exception, and Lufthansa has one of the largest first class fleets in the world.

The carrier's new A350-1000s can carry 300 passengers, and while the layout for the 777-9 has not been revealed, it's believed these planes will likely seat over 350 passengers. In addition, the airline plans to base the two at different hubs. Overall, they serve different purposes for Lufthansa and multiple other airlines. Reportedly, the airline is looking to place a new order for large widebodies, pitting the A350-1000 against the 777-9, but a split order is most likely given their complementary roles.
